summary: Discusses implementation decisions for routing in the NSFNET, especially its Backbone. A main concern is limiting routing information so that only the best route, as chosen by a policy decision, gets advertised.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo describes how the NSFNET backbone planned to exchange reachability information with regional networks. It adds agreements and checks so that routes follow each network's chosen representatives.

questions: how nsfnet chose routes to advertise
how did nsfnet use egp for policy routing
primary secondary routes in routing policy
subtitle: How NSFNET paired EGP reachability information with routing agreements.

tldr.problem: EGP alone did not let NSFNET enforce which regional networks could advertise a route or which path should be primary.
tldr.mechanism: Networks make bilateral agreements about primary and backup regional representatives; the backbone checks EGP advertisements against a routing policy database.
tldr.outcome: The memo describes an interim policy-based method for the NSFNET backbone and regional networks. Its status is listed as Unknown.

sections.title: The Routing Problem
sections.content:
The NSFNET backbone routes packets between the regional networks connected to it. The path depends on the backbone's routing method and information about external networks. This memo focuses on exchanging reachability information so packets can use a reasonable route.

The memo says EGP would be used between the backbone and regional networks, but EGP assumed a spanning-tree model and did not itself prevent false or unwanted route advertisements. It also did not provide a generally agreed way to distinguish primary and secondary paths.
sections.plainLanguage: The backbone needed to know which regional networks could reach each destination. EGP exchanged route information, but did not enforce the agreements about who should advertise a route.

sections.title: Agreements and Route Preference
sections.content:
The memo proposes a limited form of policy-based routing. A network can make bilateral agreements with one or more regional networks that will represent it to the NSFNET backbone. It may choose a primary representative and secondary ones.

The primary advertises the network with distance zero; secondary representatives use distance one or higher. If the primary path is available, the secondary paths are ignored. If it fails, the next available path with the lowest EGP metric is used.
sections.plainLanguage: Each network chooses a main regional representative and can name backups. The backbone prefers the main path and turns to a backup if that path becomes unavailable.

sections.title: Checking Advertisements
sections.content:
The NSFNET backbone Network Operation Center records agreements in a Routing Policy Data Base. The backbone periodically compares reachability information received through EGP with that database. A mismatch, such as an unapproved regional network advertising a destination, causes an alarm to the Network Operation Center.

The memo also calls for checking the autonomous system numbers advertised by regional networks. The NSFNET backbone is treated as a separate autonomous system with its own number.
sections.plainLanguage: The backbone checks route announcements against a record of the agreements. If a network advertises a route without authorization, the Network Operation Center receives an alarm.

sections.title: Backbone and Regional Expectations
sections.content:
The NSFNET backbone advertises routes to regional networks with a fixed EGP metric of 128. The memo says this may help regional networks use backdoor routes when desired and available. Regional networks can choose how to route traffic for particular destinations.

Regional networks are expected to obtain autonomous system numbers, connect to the backbone through EGP, provide metric information when needed and share copies of their agreements with the backbone management.
sections.plainLanguage: The backbone advertises the same metric for its routes, leaving regional networks free to choose available direct routes. Each regional network is expected to share its routing agreements and needed metric information.
